title: Not-for-Profit Accounting Foundations
description: Learn the purpose, reporting model, and core financial statement concepts used by not-for-profit entities.
html:
What Is a Not-for-Profit Organization?

A not-for-profit organization exists primarily to accomplish a mission rather than to generate profits for owners or shareholders.

Examples may include charities, foundations, museums, private universities, hospitals, religious organizations, and other mission-driven organizations.

The Major Reporting Difference

A business entity normally reports stockholders' equity.

A not-for-profit organization instead reports net assets.

NOT-FOR-PROFIT ASSETS − LIABILITIES = NET ASSETS

Two Classes of Net Assets

Net assets are presented in two broad classes.

Without Donor Restrictions Resources Not Subject to Donor-Imposed Restrictions
With Donor Restrictions Resources Subject to Donor-Imposed Restrictions

Donor Restrictions Matter

One of the most important questions in not-for-profit accounting is:

DID THE DONOR RESTRICT THE RESOURCE?

A donor may restrict how or when contributed resources can be used.

Example

A donor gives a charity $100,000 and requires the money to be used for a new children's education program.

The contribution is subject to a donor-imposed purpose restriction.

Unrestricted Example

Assume instead that a donor contributes $40,000 and gives the organization discretion over how to use it.

NO DONOR RESTRICTION → NET ASSETS WITHOUT DONOR RESTRICTIONS

Contributions

Contributions are an important source of support for many not-for-profit organizations.

Accounting for a contribution depends on factors such as whether the contribution is conditional and whether the donor imposed restrictions on its use.

Exchange Transaction vs. Contribution

A contribution is generally a nonreciprocal transaction.

This means the donor does not receive approximately equal value in exchange for the resources transferred.

Contribution Nonreciprocal
Exchange Transaction Reciprocal Exchange of Value
Example

A donor gives a museum $10,000 and receives nothing of comparable value.

This is generally a contribution.

If a customer instead purchases a $50 admission ticket in exchange for admission to the museum, that transaction generally has an exchange component.

Main Financial Statements

A not-for-profit organization's financial reporting generally includes:

  • Statement of Financial Position
  • Statement of Activities
  • Statement of Cash Flows
  • Information about expenses by nature and function

Statement of Financial Position

This statement reports assets, liabilities, and net assets.

ASSETS − LIABILITIES = NET ASSETS

Statement of Activities

The statement of activities reports changes in the organization's net assets during the reporting period.

It presents changes in:

  • Net assets without donor restrictions
  • Net assets with donor restrictions

Expenses

Not-for-profit organizations also report information about expenses according to their function and nature.

Function Why the Cost Was Incurred
Nature What Type of Cost It Was
Example

Employee salaries are a natural classification.

Program services and management/general activities are examples of functional classifications.

CPA Memory Rule

NFP ACCOUNTING NO OWNERS' EQUITY → NET ASSETS TWO CLASSES: WITHOUT DONOR RESTRICTIONS WITH DONOR RESTRICTIONS

Key Takeaways

  • NFPs report net assets rather than stockholders' equity.
  • Net assets are classified based on donor restrictions.
  • Contributions are generally nonreciprocal transactions.
  • Donor restrictions affect whether contribution revenue increases net assets with donor restrictions or net assets without donor restrictions.
  • Expenses are analyzed by both function and nature.

quiz.prompt: A donor gives a not-for-profit organization $75,000 and requires the organization to use the contribution exclusively for a specified educational program. How should the contribution generally be classified when recognized?
quiz.explanation: Because the donor requires the contribution to be used for a specified purpose, the contribution is subject to a donor-imposed restriction and generally increases net assets with donor restrictions.

objectives: Explain not-for-profit accounting foundations and its underlying principles.
Apply the topic to a financial-reporting scenario.
Evaluate common errors and their financial-statement effects.
